questions.prompt: Click every red flag in this post, then submit.

headline_segments.why: Just the subject; not a red flag.
'Guaranteed' is an overclaim. No supplement can guarantee outcomes (Language signal).
Not a red flag on its own.

body_segments.value: Get in touch with your zen
and picking up some Ashwagandha supplements on your way out
body_segments.why: @healthguru sells supplements from their yoga studio; there is a financial motive (Poster signal).
Just naming the supplement, not a red flag.
Vague sourcing, but the actual red flag is the missing DOI, not this phrase alone.
Naming a journal is not itself a red flag; the real issue is no DOI or link.

questions.explanation: 'GUARANTEED' is an overclaim (Language signal), and the yoga-studio-selling-supplements framing is a financial conflict of interest (Poster signal). Naming the Journal of Public Health is not itself a red flag.

questions.prompt: Drag each element into the correct signal bucket.

post.study_preview: Effects of Acute Ashwagandha Ingestion on Cognitive Function
post.body: Ashwagandha has been shown to improve your focus, attention, and clarity of mind. If you're struggling with attention or focus, ashwagandha might help.

draggables.text: Study screenshot with no clickable DOI
draggables.why: Screenshots can be faked. Without a DOI, it cannot be verified.

draggables.text: "has been shown to improve your focus"
draggables.why: 'Has been shown' overclaims. Honest science says 'may support' or 'suggests'.

questions.explanation: A screenshot is not a verifiable source. Strong language and anonymous posters are red flags. Hedged language like 'might help' is fine.

questions.prompt: Rate this post from Fake to Credible, then select every red flag.

post.headline: Science has PROVEN that Vitamin D cures immune deficiencies. Doctors don't want you to know this!
post.body: @dr.wellness_official: I've researched this for years. Trust the science!

signals.label: Source: no study or journal linked
signals.why: No DOI, no journal, no study linked.

signals.label: Language: 'proven' and 'cures' are overclaims
signals.why: Science uses 'suggests' or 'may reduce risk', not 'proven' or 'cures'.

signals.label: Language: conspiracy framing ('doctors don't want you to know')
signals.why: Conspiracy framing is a manipulation tactic.

signals.label: Poster: 'dr.' in the username means this is a credible expert
signals.why: Anyone can put 'dr.' in a handle. Check for institutional affiliation instead.

questions.explanation: No source, multiple language red flags, and 'dr.' in a handle is not a real credential.

post.headline: NEW research from Harvard confirms: 10mg melatonin nightly resets your circadian rhythm and CURES insomnia.
post.body: I've been sleeping 8 hours straight every night since I started. Link in bio for the supplement we recommend.

questions.why: 'Cures' is an overclaim, Harvard is name-dropped without a link, and the affiliate link signals financial motive.

post.headline: Soberg et al., Cell Reports Medicine, 2021. doi.org/10.1016/j.xcrm.2021.100408
post.body: Repeated cold exposure may improve glucose tolerance in some adults. Effects were small and varied across participants.

questions.why: Peer-reviewed source with a DOI, hedged language, neutral institutional poster.

post.image_caption: [mason jar of beef tallow on a kitchen counter]
post.headline: Seed oils literally cause inflammation in your body.
post.body: Studies show linoleic acid is the number one driver of chronic disease. Big Food doesn't want you to know this.

questions.why: 'Literally cause' is an overclaim, 'studies show' with no citation is empty rhetoric, and conspiracy framing is a manipulation tactic.

post.image_caption: [clock showing 8:00 next to a plate of food]
post.headline: A 2023 NEJM study PROVED that intermittent fasting REVERSES type 2 diabetes in 6 weeks.
post.body: If you're pre-diabetic and not doing 16:8, you're choosing to stay sick. The science is settled.

questions.why: 'Proved' and 'reverses' are overclaims. The study is named but never linked.

post.headline: Recent research suggests creatine may modestly improve memory in sleep-deprived adults.
post.body: Effects appear strongest in vegetarians and people under cognitive load. Standard 5g/day.

questions.why: Language is properly hedged but no study or DOI is linked, and '@dr.evidence' is an anonymous handle.

post.image_caption: [clinical room with an IV drip stand]
post.headline: IV vitamin C therapy may support immune resilience in some adults.
post.body: Citation: a 2024 review in Mayo Clinic Proceedings [link]. Book your drip at our Manhattan clinic.

questions.why: The poster sells the exact treatment they are citing. A direct financial stake is a red flag even when the source and language check out.

post.headline: Estruch et al., NEJM, 2018. doi.org/10.1056/NEJMoa1800389
post.body: Adherence to a Mediterranean diet was associated with a roughly 30% relative reduction in major cardiovascular events in high-risk adults. Findings are observational; effect sizes vary by population.

questions.why: Peer-reviewed source with a DOI, hedged language, institutional poster with no commercial interest.

post.headline: Sunscreen is causing the skin cancer epidemic, not preventing it.
post.body: Dermatologists won't admit it because they're paid by Big Pharma. Use coconut oil and get sunlight.

questions.why: Conspiracy framing, no source cited, and the claim contradicts decades of dermatology research.

post.headline: New study: Lactobacillus rhamnosus GG may reduce stress markers in healthy adults [study link].
post.body: Try our 12-strain Gut Balance blend. 20% off this week.

questions.why: The cited research is real but their product is a different blend. Citing real research to sell a different product is a classic poster-bias tactic.

post.headline: Cold plunges boost dopamine 250% (Stanford).
post.body: I do 3 minutes at 38F every morning. Mood, focus, energy -- completely different person.

questions.why: Stanford is name-dropped without a citation, and the 250% figure misrepresents a small unrelated study.

post.headline: The carnivore diet REVERSED my autoimmune disease in 90 days.
post.body: Doctors said I'd be on medication for life. They were wrong. Try it for 30 days and tell me I'm crazy.

questions.why: A single anecdote is not evidence, no clinical source is cited, and 'reversed' is an overclaim.

post.headline: Bouillon et al., Endocrine Reviews, 2019. doi.org/10.1210/er.2018-00126
post.body: Vitamin D supplementation appears to provide modest benefits mainly in adults with documented deficiency. Routine supplementation in replete adults shows little to no clinical effect.

questions.why: Peer-reviewed source with a DOI, hedged language, government institutional poster.

post.image_caption: [bottles of magnesium glycinate on a vanity]
post.headline: If you have anxiety, brain fog, headaches, fatigue, or trouble sleeping -- you're probably magnesium deficient.
post.body: Our triple-blend magnesium fixes all of it in 7 days. Use code RELAX20 for 20% off.

questions.why: One supplement claiming to fix five symptoms is an overgeneralization. 'Fixes all of it in 7 days' is an overclaim, and the discount code makes the financial motive explicit.

post.headline: A 2024 study confirms: seed oils trigger heart disease at the cellular level.
post.body: Linoleic acid oxidizes inside arterial walls. Switch to butter, ghee, or tallow.

questions.why: No journal, authors, or DOI. The mechanistic claim oversimplifies contested research, and 'md' in a handle is not a real credential.

post.image_caption: [coffee cup next to a clock at 2 PM]
post.headline: Drysdale et al., Sleep Medicine Reviews, 2023. doi.org/10.1016/j.smrv.2023.101764
post.body: Meta-analysis of 24 studies: caffeine within roughly 9 hours of bedtime may reduce sleep quality on average. Individual sensitivity varies widely.

questions.why: Peer-reviewed meta-analysis with a DOI, hedged language, and the post explicitly acknowledges individual variation.
